Declaration of Indulgence
dek-lar-ā'-shun uv in-dul'-jens
n. (the Declarations of Indulgence, 1662, 1672 and 1687–88, royal suspensions of the penal laws)
Latin declarare, to make clear; indulgentia, a granting of favour, remission.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

The Declarations of Indulgence were attempts by Charles II and James II to suspend the penal laws against Nonconformists and Roman Catholics by royal prerogative rather than by Act of Parliament. Charles issued one in 1662, withdrew it, and issued a second in 1672 which licensed over fifteen hundred Dissenting preachers before Parliament forced its cancellation in 1673. James II issued declarations in 1687 and 1688 and ordered the second read from every pulpit, which produced the trial of the Seven Bishops. The Dissenters were deeply divided over them. The relief was real and immediate — Bunyan was licensed in 1672 — but the instrument was a claim that the king could set aside a statute at will, and a liberty granted that way could be revoked the same way, as 1673 proved. Most of the leading Nonconformists refused James's indulgence, judging the price too high and the motive transparent. Their reasoning was not merely political: “Put not your trust in princes, nor in the son of man, in whom there is no help” (Psa 146:3).

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines indulgence as favour granted, and prerogative as an exclusive or peculiar privilege.

expand to see more

INDUL'GENCE, n. Favor granted; liberality; gratification; remission of the penalty.

PREROG'ATIVE, n. An exclusive or peculiar privilege; a right or power belonging to an office.

SUSPEND', v.t. To cause to cease for a time; to intermit; to stay.

Key Scripture

Psa 146:3 — "Put not your trust in princes, nor in the son of man, in whom there is no help."

Jer 17:5 — "Thus saith the LORD; Cursed be the man that trusteth in man, and maketh flesh his arm, and whose heart departeth from the LORD."

Isa 2:22 — "Cease ye from man, whose breath is in his nostrils: for wherein is he to be accounted of?"

Pro 21:1 — "The king's heart is in the hand of the LORD, as the rivers of water: he turneth it whithersoever he will."

Modern Corruption

Royal suspensions of the penal laws, which the Dissenters mostly refused to buy.

expand to see more

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The Indulgences pose a question churches still face: whether to accept relief from an authority acting outside its own law, when the relief is genuine and urgently needed. Fifteen hundred licences in 1672 meant preaching, and the cancellation of 1673 meant prison again. The men who refused in 1687 were not ungrateful; they had learned what a prerogative gift is worth.

The principle to recover is where a church's confidence rests. “Cursed be the man that trusteth in man, and maketh flesh his arm” (Jer 17:5) is not a counsel of political withdrawal, since the king's heart is still in the LORD's hand (Pro 21:1); it is a warning against making a patron's favour the ground of the church's standing.

Usage

"“Put not your trust in princes” (Psa 146:3) — why most refused James's indulgence."

"“Cursed be the man that trusteth in man, and maketh flesh his arm” (Jer 17:5) — a prerogative liberty."

"“Cease ye from man, whose breath is in his nostrils” (Isa 2:22) — 1672 and then 1673."
